passage:
For six weeks after we started meeting, I didn't know what Lavanya and I were. We'd go to the old bookshop on Saturdays and text every night, and then she'd mention a "coffee with someone from the gym" and I'd spend the evening guessing.
Manoj finally said, "Dhruv, you're writing thesis-length theories. Just ask her."
So last Sunday, walking back from the bookshop, I said it, badly rehearsed: "I'd like us to be only seeing each other. Where are you on that?" My ears were burning.
She stopped walking. "I was hoping you'd ask," she said. "The gym person is my cousin's friend. I wasn't sure what you wanted either."
Even now I think: if she'd said no, it would have hurt, but at least I'd have stopped guessing. Asking was the scariest ten seconds of the year. And the most useful.

qa.q: Where were Dhruv and Lavanya walking back from when Dhruv asked?
qa.a: They were walking back from the bookshop.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel while asking, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Dhruv was nervous; the words came out badly rehearsed and Dhruv's ears were burning. 😅

qa.q: Why was asking directly better than more guessing?
qa.a: Asking risked a no, but it ended six weeks of theories and gave both of them facts to act on; it also showed Lavanya had been unsure too.

qa.q: What had Lavanya been feeling during those six weeks?
qa.a: Lavanya was also unsure what Dhruv wanted and was hoping Dhruv would ask.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking directly to be exclusive, risking a no to end weeks of guessing.

passage:
Counselling note. Final-year student Rashmi, sessions 3 and 4.
Session 3: Rashmi said she and Jeevan have been meeting for two months, but she doesn't know if they are "a thing". She checks whether he posts photos with other people and loses sleep over his vague replies. We discussed that the uncertainty is costing her more than an answer would. She wrote her own sentence and practised it twice: "I like you and I'd like us to be exclusive. What do you want?"
Session 4, a week later: Rashmi said she asked him on the walk back from the metro. Jeevan said he wasn't ready for anything exclusive yet. She cried that night, she told me, but by the next day felt "weirdly lighter". "At least I'm not reading tea leaves any more." She has decided to step back from seeing him. She seemed sad but steady.

qa.q: What did Jeevan say when Rashmi asked?
qa.a: Jeevan said he wasn't ready for anything exclusive yet.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi feel 'weirdly lighter' after hearing no?
qa.a: The answer hurt, but it ended the guessing; Rashmi no longer had to read every vague reply for meaning.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Rashmi prepare?
qa.a: The counsellor helped Rashmi see the cost of uncertainty and let her write and practise her own clear sentence, so she could ask directly.

qa.q: What might the question have been like from Jeevan's side?
qa.a: Jeevan may have felt awkward, but a clear question made it easier to give a clear answer instead of more vague replies.

grounding: Illustrates a student asking directly about exclusivity and acting on the answer, even though it is a no.

passage:
Wednesday night

I did it. I asked Nikhil.

We've been going out for two months and I've been going crazy. Is he seeing other people? Are we a thing? Charu kept saying, "Just ask him, Kavitha, stop guessing." So after dinner, on the bench outside the hostel, I said it: "I'd like us to be exclusive. Where are you on that?"

My heart was pounding so hard I thought he could hear it.

He was quiet for a moment. Then he said, "I thought we already were. But I'm glad you asked."

I laughed so loudly the guard looked over. 😅

Even if he'd said no, I think I'd have been okay. At least I'd know. Two months of guessing was worse than any answer.

qa.q: Where did Kavitha ask Nikhil the question?
qa.a: On the bench outside the hostel, after dinner.

qa.q: How was Kavitha feeling just before Nikhil answered?
qa.a: Kavitha was nervous, her heart pounding, afraid of hearing a no.

qa.q: Why did asking directly help Kavitha, whatever the answer?
qa.a: It ended two months of guessing, so Kavitha could act on facts instead of worry.

qa.q: How might Nikhil have felt when Kavitha asked?
qa.a: He may have been a little surprised but pleased, since he already thought they were exclusive, and glad she said it aloud.

grounding: Kavitha directly asks Nikhil about being exclusive, risking a no to end weeks of guessing, and finds relief in knowing where they stand.

passage:
Sachin: Hey. Can I ask you something kind of serious?

Joseph: uh oh. go ahead

Sachin: We've been seeing each other for almost three months. I really like you. I'd like us to be exclusive. Where do you stand?

Joseph: ...

Joseph: okay this is a lot over text 😅

Sachin: I know. I just didn't want to keep guessing. Honest answer is fine, even if it's a no.

Joseph: honest answer: I like you a lot too. but I'm not ready to say exclusive yet. I got out of something bad last year

Sachin: Okay. Thank you for telling me.

Joseph: are you upset

Sachin: A little. But I'd rather know. Can we talk properly on Saturday?

Joseph: yes. and Sachin, thanks for asking straight. most people don't

Sachin: 🙂

qa.q: How long have Sachin and Joseph been seeing each other?
qa.a: Almost three months.

qa.q: How does Sachin feel after Joseph's answer?
qa.a: Sachin feels a little upset and disappointed, but also relieved to know where things stand.

qa.q: Why was asking directly still worth it, even though the answer was not yes?
qa.a: It ended the guessing and gave both of them facts to act on, and led to a plan to talk properly on Saturday.

qa.q: How does Joseph see Sachin's direct question?
qa.a: Joseph appreciates it, saying most people don't ask straight, even though the timing felt like a lot.

grounding: Sachin asks Joseph directly about being exclusive, risks and receives a "not yet", and both can now act on facts rather than guesses.

passage:
Shankar had been seeing Leela for ten weeks, mostly at the weekly market in their small town in Kerala, where she ran her father's spice stall and he ran the phone repair shop across the lane.

Everyone in the lane had opinions. Thomas from the tea shop kept asking, "So? Is it serious or not?" and Shankar never knew what to say.

On Thursday evening, after the market closed, he helped Leela stack the empty sacks. Then he said, "Leela. I don't want to see anyone else. I'd like it to be just us. What about you?"

She stopped stacking. "You're asking me? Here? Among the sacks?"

"I couldn't wait for a better place."

She laughed. Then she said, "I need to think about it. My father..."

"That's okay. At least now I know you know."

Walking home, he felt oddly light.

qa.q: What did Leela run at the weekly market?
qa.a: Her father's spice stall.

qa.q: Why does Shankar feel oddly light walking home, even without a yes?
qa.a: He feels relieved because he finally asked and ended the guessing, even though Leela needs time.

qa.q: What did Shankar's direct question achieve?
qa.a: It made his wish clear and let Leela respond honestly, so both could now act on facts rather than on the lane's opinions.

qa.q: What might be on Leela's mind when she says "My father..."?
qa.a: She is probably torn, liking Shankar but worried about her father's reaction and what it would mean at home.

grounding: In a small Kerala town Shankar asks Leela directly to be exclusive, risking a no to end weeks of guessing, and feels lighter for knowing where they stand.

passage: The laundromat on Queen Street smelled of warm cotton and cheap soap. Bao watched her socks tumble and made herself say it before the dryer stopped. "Abebe, we've been seeing each other for six weeks. I'd like us to be exclusive. Where do you stand?" He looked up from folding a towel, eyebrows high. For a long second only the machines spoke. Bao's heart hammered; she had rehearsed this on the tram and still her voice wobbled at the end. "I was hoping you'd ask," he said slowly, "because I was scared to. Yes. I'd like that." She laughed, mostly from relief. "I was ready for a no, you know. I just couldn't keep guessing every time you didn't text back." He handed her the warm towel. "No more guessing, then."

qa.q: Where was Bao when she asked Abebe where he stood?
qa.a: She was at the laundromat on Queen Street, watching her socks tumble in the dryer.

qa.q: What was Bao feeling in the long second before Abebe answered?
qa.a: She was nervous and scared of a no; her heart hammered and her voice wobbled, and then she laughed with relief.

qa.q: Why did asking directly work better for Bao than waiting?
qa.a: It risked a no, but it ended the guessing over unanswered texts, so both of them could act on a clear answer.

qa.q: How does Abebe experience Bao's question?
qa.a: Abebe is relieved and glad, because he had wanted the same thing but had been too scared to ask it himself.

grounding: Shows one partner asking directly about exclusivity, accepting the risk of a no in exchange for an end to weeks of guessing.
